learn.hook: Your pocket money is gone by the 10th of every month, and you cannot remember where it went. A budget is the detective that finds out!
points: A budget is a plan of expected income and spending for a period such as a week, a month or a year.
Income is the money coming in, such as a salary, pocket money, business profit or interest. Expenses are the money going out.

Fixed expenses stay about the same each month (rent, school fees, a loan instalment). Variable expenses change (groceries, electricity, outings). Needs, such as food, shelter, medicines and education, come before wants.
If income is more than expenses, the budget has a surplus. If expenses are more than income, it has a deficit. If the two are equal, it is balanced.
'Pay yourself first': set aside savings as soon as money comes in, then spend the rest. Tracking every expense shows where money leaks away.

example.q: Think it through: The Sharma family in Jaipur earns ₹40,000 a month. They spend ₹12,000 on rent, ₹9,000 on groceries, ₹5,000 on school fees, ₹2,500 on electricity and phone, ₹3,000 on travel and ₹2,500 on outings. Is their budget in surplus or deficit?
steps: Income is more than expenses, so the budget has a surplus.
The family can save the ₹6,000 or keep part of it for emergencies.

learn.reallife: Families plan monthly household budgets, schools plan for annual functions, and the Government of India presents a budget in Parliament every year.

games.title: Need or want?
items: Medicines prescribed by a doctor
Rice and dal for the family
Monthly house rent
School fees
A fourth pair of headphones
The newest video game
A movie ticket for the weekend
An expensive designer watch

items.q: Income ₹500, spending ₹420: surplus of how many rupees?
Income ₹1,000, spending ₹1,150: deficit of how many rupees?
Income ₹2,000, spending ₹2,000: what kind of budget?
Spending on outings: fixed or variable expense?

quiz.q: What is a budget?
options: A list of things you want to buy someday
A plan of expected income and spending for a period
quiz.explain: A budget plans how much money will come in and how it will be spent or saved over a week, month or year.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a budget is only a shopping wish list

quiz.q: Neha's family earns ₹30,000 a month and spends ₹27,500. What is their monthly surplus?
quiz.explain: Surplus = income − expenses = ₹30,000 − ₹27,500 = ₹2,500.
quiz.mistake: Adds income and spending, or gives the spending itself

quiz.q: When expenses are more than income, the budget is said to be:
quiz.explain: A deficit means spending is more than income, so the gap must be covered by savings or borrowing.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the words surplus and deficit

quiz.q: Which of these is usually a fixed expense for a family?
quiz.explain: Rent stays the same every month, so it is a fixed expense. Restaurant meals, gifts and electricity use change from month to month.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any essential expense is fixed, even if its amount changes

quiz.q: Which of these is a need rather than a want?
options: A medicine prescribed by a doctor
A costly pair of designer sunglasses
quiz.explain: Needs are things we must have to live safely and healthily, such as food, shelter, medicines and education.
quiz.mistake: Treats things we desire as things we cannot do without

quiz.q: What does 'pay yourself first' mean?
options: Spend all your money on yourself
Put aside savings as soon as you receive money, before spending
Pay others only after buying wants
quiz.explain: Saving first makes sure savings actually happen, instead of saving only what is left at the end of the month.
quiz.mistake: Takes the phrase to mean spending on yourself

quiz.q: Aditya gets ₹1,500 pocket money a month. He spends ₹600 on snacks, ₹300 on mobile recharge and ₹400 on comics. How much is left for saving?
quiz.mistake: Gives the total spending instead of what is left

items: Snacks
Recharge
Comics
Left

quiz.q: Why is it useful to track every expense for a month?
options: It shows where money is being spent so you can cut waste
quiz.explain: Tracking reveals small 'leaks', such as frequent snacks, that add up. Then you can plan better.
quiz.mistake: Thinks tracking spending changes income or prices

teach.ask: Gappu is upset: "My seed money always runs out before the month ends! What is a budget, and how will it help me?"
teach.praise: Chirp! A budget plans my income and my spending, puts needs first and saves some money at the start. No more empty seed jars!
teach.nudge: You told me about spending. But what about the money coming in, and how do I make sure I save some?

learn.hook: Put ₹1,000 in a bank and do nothing. A year later there is more than ₹1,000. Where did the extra money come from?
points: Saving means keeping aside the part of income that is not spent today, for goals such as education, a bicycle or emergencies. An emergency fund is money kept ready for sudden needs like illness or repairs.
Banks keep savings safe and pay interest. A savings account lets you take money out any time. A fixed deposit locks money for a fixed period and usually pays a higher rate of interest.
Simple interest is paid only on the original amount (the principal): Simple interest = Principal × Rate × Time ÷ 100.
Compound interest is paid on the principal plus the interest already earned, so money grows faster over time. Starting to save early gives compounding more time to work.
Inflation is a general rise in prices over time. It lowers the purchasing power of money, so savings should ideally grow faster than prices rise.

example.q: Think it through: Isha puts ₹5,000 in a bank at 10% interest a year for 2 years. How much interest does she earn with simple interest, and with interest compounded yearly?
steps: Compound interest, year 1: 10% of ₹5,000 = ₹500, so she has ₹5,500.
Year 2: 10% of ₹5,500 = ₹550, so she has ₹6,050. Total interest = ₹1,050.
Compound interest gives ₹50 more because in year 2 she also earns interest on the first year's interest.

learn.reallife: A piggy bank keeps coins safe but adds nothing, while a bank savings account or a recurring deposit, which many parents open for children's goals, earns interest.

games.title: Money words
pairs: The original amount saved or borrowed
Extra money paid for the use of money
Money locked in a bank for a fixed period
A general rise in prices over time
Savings kept ready for sudden needs

items.text: Interest earned on earlier interest is called ___ interest.
When prices rise, the purchasing power of money ___.
Money kept aside for sudden needs like illness is an ___ fund.

quiz.q: Raj saves ₹2,000 in a bank at 5% simple interest per year. How much interest does he earn in 3 years?
quiz.explain: Simple interest = 2,000 × 5 × 3 ÷ 100 = ₹300.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to multiply by the time, or forgets to divide by 100

quiz.q: ₹1,000 is deposited at 10% interest per year, compounded yearly. What is the amount after 2 years?
quiz.mistake: Uses simple interest and forgets interest on the first year's interest

quiz.q: Why does money grow faster with compound interest than with simple interest at the same rate?
options: Interest is also earned on the interest already added
The bank changes the principal every day
Simple interest is paid only once in a lifetime
quiz.explain: With compounding, each year's interest is added to the principal, so the next year's interest is calculated on a bigger amount.
quiz.mistake: Does not see that interest itself starts earning interest

quiz.q: A school bag costs ₹200 this year. If its price rises by 10% in a year, what will it cost next year?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts instead of adds, or takes 10% as ₹10

quiz.q: What happens to the purchasing power of ₹100 when there is inflation?
options: It falls, because ₹100 buys fewer goods than before
It rises, because prices are higher
quiz.explain: When prices rise, the same amount of money buys less. So inflation reduces purchasing power.
quiz.mistake: Thinks higher prices make money more valuable

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of an emergency fund?
options: To pay for sudden needs like illness or urgent repairs
To lend money to friends for games
quiz.explain: An emergency fund protects a family from having to borrow when something unexpected happens.
quiz.mistake: Confuses savings for emergencies with savings for wants

quiz.q: How is a fixed deposit different from a savings account?
options: A fixed deposit pays no interest
Money in a fixed deposit can be withdrawn any time without any rule
A fixed deposit keeps money for a fixed period and usually pays higher interest
A fixed deposit is kept at home
quiz.explain: In a fixed deposit, money is locked for an agreed period, and in return the bank usually pays a higher rate than on a savings account.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the features of the two kinds of deposits

quiz.q: Tara and Vikram save the same amount every year at the same compound interest rate. Tara starts at 25 and Vikram at 35. Who is likely to have more at 60?
options: Both will have exactly the same
Tara, because her money has more years to compound
quiz.explain: Tara saves for more years, and her money has 10 extra years to earn interest on interest. Starting early is a big advantage.
quiz.mistake: Does not see how time multiplies the effect of compounding

teach.ask: Gappu holds up a coin: "Should I hide my coin under my nest or put it in a bank? How can my money grow?"
teach.praise: Tweet! In a bank my coin earns interest, and with compound interest even the interest earns interest. I will start saving early!
teach.nudge: If I keep it in the bank, what extra money will I get? And does it matter how early I start?

topics.title: Financial literacy: borrowing, risk and staying safe

learn.hook: "Congratulations! You have won ₹50,000. Just share the OTP sent to your phone." Would you share it? A financially smart person never would!
points: Financial literacy means having the knowledge and skills to earn, spend, save, borrow and invest money wisely.

A loan must be repaid with interest. Banks are regulated by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), and formal lenders such as banks and cooperatives usually charge lower interest than informal moneylenders. Borrow only what you can repay.
Higher returns usually come with higher risk. Spreading savings across different options (diversification) reduces risk: don't put all your eggs in one basket.
Insurance protects against big losses. You pay a small regular amount (premium), and the insurer pays if the insured loss, such as illness or crop damage, happens.

Stay safe: never share your OTP, PIN, CVV or passwords; banks never ask for them. You do not need to enter your UPI PIN to receive money. Offers that promise to double money quickly are likely frauds. Report cyber fraud on the national helpline 1930.

example.q: Think it through: Rohan gets an SMS: "You have won a lottery of ₹50,000! Click this link and share the OTP to claim it." He never bought a lottery ticket. What should he do?
steps: He did not enter any lottery, so the 'prize' cannot be real.
An OTP is a secret code that lets someone approve a transaction from his account. Sharing it could let a fraudster take his money.
He should not click the link or share the OTP, and should delete the message.
He should tell a parent and, if any money is lost, report it quickly on the cyber fraud helpline 1930.
example.answer: Ignore the message, never share the OTP or click the link, tell an adult and report fraud on 1930 if needed.

learn.reallife: Families compare loan interest rates before buying a scooter, farmers buy crop insurance before the sowing season, and shopkeepers check payment messages before handing over goods.

games.title: Smart move or risky move?
items: Keeping your UPI PIN secret
Comparing interest rates before taking a loan
Buying health insurance for the family
Spreading savings across different options
Sharing an OTP with a caller who says he is from the bank
Putting all savings into a scheme that promises to double money in a month
Borrowing more than you can repay
Clicking a prize link from an unknown sender

games.title: True or false?
items: You need to enter your UPI PIN to receive money.
A UPI PIN is needed only to send or pay money, never to receive it.
Banks never ask customers for their OTP or PIN over a call.
Anyone asking for them is likely a fraudster.
A loan has to be repaid along with interest.
Interest is the cost of using borrowed money.
Diversification means putting all your savings in one place.
Diversification means spreading savings to reduce risk.
An insurance premium is the amount you pay to the insurer.
In return, the insurer covers the insured losses.
Schemes that promise to double your money in a few weeks are safe investments.
Such promises are a common sign of fraud.

quiz.q: A caller says he is from your bank and asks for the OTP sent to your phone to 'update your account'. What should you do?
options: Refuse, end the call and inform a parent or the bank
quiz.explain: Banks never ask for OTPs. Sharing it could let the caller take money from the account.
quiz.mistake: Trusts a caller just because he claims to be from the bank

quiz.q: Your friend wants to send you ₹200 through UPI. What do you need to enter to receive it?
options: Nothing; no PIN is needed to receive money
quiz.explain: You need a UPI PIN only to pay. A request asking you to enter your PIN to 'receive' money is a trick.
quiz.mistake: Believes a PIN is needed to receive money

quiz.q: Why is borrowing from a bank usually better than borrowing from an informal moneylender?
options: Banks are regulated by the RBI and usually charge lower interest
quiz.explain: Formal lenders follow RBI rules and usually charge lower interest. Informal lenders may charge very high interest and are not regulated in the same way.
quiz.mistake: Does not see the difference between formal and informal credit

quiz.q: Mr. Iyer borrows ₹10,000 from a bank at 12% simple interest for 1 year. How much must he repay in total at the end of the year?
quiz.mistake: Gives only the interest, or forgets to add the principal

quiz.q: What is an insurance premium?
options: The amount the insurer pays after a loss
The regular amount paid to the insurer for cover
quiz.explain: You pay the premium regularly. In return, the insurance company pays you if an insured loss happens.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the premium paid with the claim received

quiz.q: Meena splits her savings between a fixed deposit, a recurring deposit and a little in other options. What is this called?
quiz.explain: Diversification spreads money across options, so a loss in one does not wipe out everything.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the term for spreading risk

quiz.q: A scheme promises to double your money in just one month with 'no risk'. What is the most sensible view?
options: It is very likely a fraud, because high returns come with high risk
It is a safe bank deposit
Everyone should put all their savings in it
quiz.explain: Very high returns with no risk do not exist. Such promises are a common sign of a fraud.
quiz.mistake: Believes in returns that sound too good to be true

quiz.q: What is the national helpline number to report cyber financial fraud in India?
quiz.explain: 1930 is the national cyber fraud helpline. Reporting quickly gives the best chance of stopping the money from being taken away.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with other emergency or child helplines

teach.ask: Gappu got a call: "Share your OTP and win a golden nest!" He asks: "How do I stay safe with money?"
teach.praise: Chirp! Never share my OTP or PIN, treat 'too good to be true' offers as scams, and report fraud on 1930. My golden nest can wait!
teach.nudge: But should I tell that caller my OTP? And what should I do if something goes wrong?
